 1. Synology DS925+: best NAS for simple remote access and backups

 Why choose the DS925+?
 Four drive bays provide more growth and RAID choices than a two-bay unit.
 DSM integrates storage management, users, shared folders, backups, file sharing, and photo workflows.
 Synology’s QuickConnect ecosystem is designed to simplify remote access without requiring manual port forwarding in typical setups.
 Two M.2 NVMe slots can support the functions allowed by the exact model and DSM version.
 A DX525 expansion unit is supported in selected markets, according to the DS925+ specification sheet .
 How does remote access work on Synology?
 Synology combines DSM, first-party mobile applications, backup tools, file-sharing features, and QuickConnect-style access. Synology documentation describes QuickConnect access without manually configuring port forwarding and uses a QuickConnect ID or address format; however, the retrieved documentation is for Synology Router Manager, so the exact DSM menu path should be checked on the current DS925+ software before publication.
 For a typical beginner setup, create separate user accounts, enable MFA where supported, install the current DSM updates, configure the official file and backup applications, and test access using cellular data rather than the home Wi-Fi.
 What is the DS925+ reservation?
 The DS925+ should not be called the best Plex NAS without qualification. The exact processor and software stack may be less attractive for on-the-fly video transcoding than an Intel-based alternative. Direct play can still work very well when the remote client supports the stored video and audio formats. Buyers should also check the current supported-drive list, drive-compatibility policy, NVMe functions, and expansion requirements because those details can materially change the total cost.
 Buy the DS925+ if: guided backups, polished administration, family file sharing, and a managed personal cloud matter more than maximum hardware specifications.
 Skip it if: you specifically need hardware-assisted transcoding, built-in 10GbE, or the highest compute performance per dollar.

QNAP also positions the TS-464 for file management, backups, collaboration, video conversion, and remote access.
 Why is the TS-464 suitable for media?
 The Intel platform makes the TS-464 a more plausible candidate for hardware-assisted media workloads than a NAS selected only for file serving. That does not guarantee a particular number of Plex or Jellyfin streams. Codec support, subtitles, client compatibility, software version, hardware acceleration settings, and remote bandwidth determine the result.
 Direct play means the client plays the stored file without conversion. Direct stream generally changes the container or delivery path without converting the video itself. Transcoding converts video or audio because the client cannot play the original format or because bandwidth requires a smaller version. A NAS can be excellent at direct play while being a poor transcoding platform.

 Is RAID a backup? 
 RAID is not a backup. RAID can keep a NAS available after some drive failures, but RAID does not restore files deleted by mistake or encrypted by ransomware, and RAID does not protect against theft, fire, account compromise, enclosure failure, or a damaged filesystem.
 A practical home arrangement has a primary NAS copy, a separate backup copy, and ideally an off-site or cloud copy. Snapshots can provide fast recovery from accidental changes or some ransomware incidents, but snapshots stored on the same NAS are not an independent backup.
 Four-bay arrays provide more RAID choices, but large drives can make rebuilds lengthy and a degraded array is more vulnerable during rebuilding. A second drive failure or an unreadable sector can turn a recoverable failure into data loss. Configure backup jobs before storing irreplaceable data on the NAS.

 Use these safe defaults
 Update the NAS operating system and applications before enabling remote access.
 Create a long, unique administrator password and use a separate non-admin account for everyday work.
 Enable MFA for vendor and NAS accounts where supported, and store recovery codes securely.
 Disable unused services, accounts, packages, and guest access.
 Use shared-folder permissions based on least privilege rather than giving every account administrator rights.
 Prefer the vendor relay service or a well-maintained VPN overlay over direct port forwarding.
 Avoid casually enabling UPnP port forwarding.
 Configure notifications for failed logins, disk errors, backup failures, and critical updates.
 Test file access from cellular data, not only from the home Wi-Fi.
 Confirm that shared links expire and require passwords when appropriate.
 A VPN overlay such as Tailscale can be useful for technically confident users who want private access without publishing NAS services, but VPN setup and maintenance are not identical across NAS brands and models.

 A 10GbE NAS cannot overcome a slow residential upload connection. Relay connections can also be slower than local, direct-WAN, or VPN connections. QNAP states that myQNAPcloud Link may apply bandwidth controls for fair use in its remote-access bandwidth FAQ .
 What is the safest remote-access setup for a beginner? 
 Install the latest stable NAS update.
 Configure the vendor’s official relay-based remote-access service.
 Create separate accounts for each household member.
 Use MFA and strong unique passwords.
 Grant access only to required shared folders.
 Disable unused applications and services.
 Do not expose the administration interface with automatic UPnP port forwarding.
 Test file access and a backup from outside the home.
 Set login-failure, disk-health, update, and backup notifications.
 Keep an independent backup before treating the NAS as the home’s only copy.
 How do QNAP users configure remote access? 
 QNAP’s documented setup begins by creating a QNAP ID, signing in to the NAS as administrator, opening myQNAPcloud , selecting Get Started , associating the NAS with the QNAP ID, and configuring access control and enabled services. Users can then connect through the generated SmartURL or myQNAPcloud website and use appropriate QNAP mobile applications. The QNAP QTS remote-access instructions provide the documented workflow.
 QNAP’s myQNAPcloud Link can use relay or NAT traversal when a direct connection is not possible. DDNS is different: DDNS maps a changing public IP address to a hostname, but DDNS is not a VPN and does not itself secure the NAS. A direct connection should be treated as an advanced configuration requiring HTTPS, MFA, updates, firewall controls, and a rollback plan.
 Which NAS should you buy for Plex or Jellyfin? 
 Choose the QNAP TS-464 when media applications, Intel-based hardware acceleration, HDMI, and broader application flexibility are more important than the simplest setup. The TerraMaster F4-424 Pro and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus are also stronger candidates for technically confident media-server users because their cited hardware is aimed at higher compute or networking workloads.
 Choose the Synology DS925+ when most media will be played by compatible clients using direct play and the household values easier backups and administration. Do not promise a specific number of 4K or remote streams without current testing or model-and-codec-specific documentation. Subtitles, unsupported audio, unsupported containers, and limited remote bandwidth can trigger transcoding even when the NAS appears powerful enough.
 What does a complete NAS budget include? 
 The enclosure is only the starting cost. Most NAS devices in this comparison are diskless, so a complete purchase may also require NAS-rated hard drives, a separate backup drive or cloud-storage subscription, a UPS, and a 2.5GbE or 10GbE switch and adapters.
 For NAS-rated hard drives, compare current models such as Seagate IronWolf and Western Digital Red Plus against the NAS manufacturer’s supported-drive list. For power protection, a UPS from APC or CyberPower can give the NAS time to shut down cleanly during an outage. Cloud or off-site copies can use a service such as Backblaze B2 or Wasabi , subject to current pricing, compatibility, and egress terms.
 Final decision tree 
 Want the simplest managed personal cloud? Start with the Synology DS925+. Choose the DS225+ if two bays are enough.
 Want media flexibility, HDMI, PCIe, and 2.5GbE? Choose the QNAP TS-464, or the TS-264 when two bays are sufficient.
 Want maximum hardware value? Compare the TerraMaster F4-424 Pro and UGREEN DXP4800 Plus, accepting more software and remote-access uncertainty.
 Want a flexible alternative ecosystem? Consider the ASUSTOR Lockerstor 4 Gen2 class after verifying the exact AS6704T specifications.
 Need future expansion or several workloads? Prefer four bays over two.
 Need only mirrored files and backups? A two-bay NAS is adequate, but budget for an independent backup.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Can I access a NAS remotely without port forwarding?
 Yes. Vendor relay services such as Synology QuickConnect-style access, QNAP myQNAPcloud Link, and UGREENlink can provide remote access without manually forwarding ports in suitable configurations. A VPN overlay is another option for users willing to manage additional setup.
 Is DDNS the same as a VPN for NAS remote access?
 No. DDNS maps a changing public IP address to a hostname, while a VPN creates an authenticated encrypted connection. DDNS alone does not secure a NAS or hide exposed services.
 Is a NAS safer than cloud storage?
 A NAS gives you more control over storage and access, but safety depends on updates, MFA, permissions, backups, router configuration, and remote-access design. A NAS located in the same home is not protected from theft, fire, ransomware, or major hardware failure without an independent or off-site copy.
 Do I need 10GbE to access my NAS remotely?
 No. 10GbE mainly improves compatible local-network transfers. Remote access is usually limited by the home internet upload speed, remote network, relay or VPN path, and client device.
 How many drive bays should a home NAS have?
 Two bays are suitable for modest personal files, phone photos, and mirrored storage. Four bays are a better long-term choice for growing libraries, several computers, surveillance, multiple services, or greater RAID flexibility.
 The Bottom Line 
 For most households, buy the Synology DS925+ when simple remote files, photo storage, sharing, and backups matter most. Choose the QNAP TS-464 for stronger media and application flexibility, and compare TerraMaster, UGREEN, or ASUSTOR when hardware value or networking matters more than the most polished software. Whatever the enclosure, use MFA, avoid casually exposing the NAS to the internet, and maintain an independent backup.

Self-hosted Dropbox alternatives: 6 open-source options | opentools.dev Skip to content If you want Dropbox on your own server, Nextcloud is the safest default: it syncs files on every platform and adds calendars, contacts and office editing if you want them. OpenCloud is the leaner pick when you only care about files, and Seafile is the one to look at for large libraries with many small files. If you don't want a server at all, Syncthing syncs your devices directly with each other.
 The rest of this guide goes through each option, what it is good at and where it gets annoying.
 What to look for in a Dropbox replacement
 Dropbox does three things most people rely on without thinking about it. It keeps a folder in sync across computers, it uploads photos from your phone, and it gives you share links for people who don't have an account. Any replacement should cover the ones you actually use.
 Before picking a tool, answer a few questions for yourself:
 Do you need share links for outsiders, or only sync between your own devices?
 Do you want to edit Word and Excel files in the browser?
 Will a family or a team use it, with their own logins?
 How much server can you spare? A Raspberry Pi and a rented VPS with 8 GB of RAM lead to different answers.
 Nextcloud
 Nextcloud is the big one, with about 37,000 GitHub stars (October 2026) and a commit history that has not slowed down. It is licensed under the AGPL-3.0 and written in PHP.
 Files are the core, but Nextcloud is closer to a self-hosted Google Workspace than to Dropbox. There are apps for calendars, contacts, mail, chat and video calls (Nextcloud Talk), plus hundreds more in its app store. The desktop and mobile clients handle several accounts, and the mobile apps can upload photos and videos automatically. Nextcloud Office lets you edit documents in the browser, and you can connect Collabora Online instead if you prefer.
 The official installation method is Nextcloud All-in-One, a single Docker command that starts a "mastercontainer" and lets you switch on Nextcloud Office, Talk and BorgBackup-based backups from a web interface.
 What it needs: the admin manual asks for at least 128 MB of RAM per PHP process and recommends 512 MB, plus MariaDB or PostgreSQL (SQLite only for tests and very small setups). In practice, Nextcloud with Office and a few active users wants a real server, not a leftover Pi.
 The downside is that size. Nextcloud has many moving parts, and upgrades across major versions need some care. If you only want sync, it may be more than you need.
 OpenCloud
 OpenCloud is a fork of ownCloud Infinite Scale, the Go rewrite of ownCloud. The Heinlein Group in Berlin took over development in early 2025 after many of the oCIS developers left ownCloud. It has about 6,100 GitHub stars (October 2026), released v8.1.0 on 5 October 2026 and is licensed under Apache 2.0.
 The interesting part is the architecture. The README says plainly: "The OpenCloud backend does not use a database. It stores all data in the filesystem." That makes backups simpler, because you copy a folder instead of coordinating a database dump with the file store.
 It is also light. The documented minimum for up to 10 users is a 1 GHz single-core CPU and 512 MB of RAM, the class of a Raspberry Pi 3. For up to 1,000 users the docs list a 2 GHz dual-core CPU and 8 GB of RAM.
 OpenCloud has a desktop sync client and apps for Android and iOS, Spaces for team folders, public links and a File Drop for uploads from outsiders. Office editing works through Collabora, and the admin docs also cover calendars and contacts through Radicale.
 It does fewer things than Nextcloud, and that is the point. If you want a file cloud and nothing else, OpenCloud is worth a test run.
 Seafile
 Seafile has about 15,000 GitHub stars (October 2026). The server core is AGPL-3.0, the web interface (Seahub) is Apache 2.0.
 Seafile organizes files into libraries and stores them in a data model similar to Git: commits, file objects and blocks. Files are cut into content-defined chunks, so unchanged parts are reused between versions and only the changed blocks need storing. The trade-off is that your files on the server are not plain files you can browse with ls . You get them out through Seafile.
 Libraries can be encrypted with a password. With the desktop client, encryption and decryption happen on your computer, so the server admin cannot read file contents. The manual is honest about the limits: file names and sizes stay visible, and when you open an encrypted library in the browser, the server does the decryption.
 Clients exist for Windows, macOS and Linux, plus a drive client called SeaDrive that shows server files like a network drive without syncing everything to disk. The Android and iOS apps are in the usual stores, and the Android app is also on F-Droid. Collabora Online and OnlyOffice integrations are documented, and SeaDoc adds collaborative documents.
 The Community Edition asks for 2 CPU cores and 2 GB of RAM. A Professional Edition with extra features such as full-text search is sold separately.
 Syncthing
 Syncthing works differently from everything else here. "There is no central server that might be compromised," as its website puts it. Your devices connect to each other directly, encrypted with TLS, and each device is identified by a certificate.
 It has about 89,000 GitHub stars (October 2026), uses the MPL-2.0 license and runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, the BSDs and more. On Android you use a community-built app.
 What you lose is the web part. There are no share links and no browser interface for your files, only a local admin page. If you mostly want your laptop, desktop and phone to have the same folders, Syncthing is the simplest and most private option on this list. It helps to run it on one always-on machine too, so there is a copy online when your other devices are off.
 Pydio Cells
 Pydio Cells is a file sharing platform written in Go, with about 2,300 GitHub stars (October 2026) and an AGPL-3.0 license. It describes itself as "open-core": the free Cells Home edition covers file sharing and collaboration, and the paid Connect and Enterprise tiers add enterprise SSO, compliance tooling and multi-tenancy. In the browser you can co-edit documents with Collabora Online or OnlyOffice.
 Pydio is aimed at companies more than at households. If you run it for a team and might later pay for support, it fits. For a family cloud, Nextcloud or OpenCloud will feel more at home.
 FileBrowser Quantum
 Sometimes you don't need sync at all, only a web page where you can upload, download and share files on a server. FileBrowser Quantum does that. It is a large fork of the original File Browser, which was archived on 1 September 2026 and no longer gets security fixes, so use the fork for new setups.
 It supports share links with expiry and permissions, OIDC and LDAP logins, two-factor authentication and fast search. There is no desktop sync client. It is licensed under Apache 2.0.
 If you need it next to other apps, it is a good companion to Syncthing: Syncthing keeps the folder in sync, FileBrowser Quantum gives you a browser view and links.
 Comparison table
 Nextcloud OpenCloud Seafile Syncthing Pydio Cells FileBrowser Quantum 
 Sync client Desktop + mobile Desktop + mobile Desktop, SeaDrive, mobile Every device runs Syncthing Native + mobile apps None (web only) 
 Share links Yes Yes Yes No Yes Yes 
 Office in browser Nextcloud Office, Collabora Collabora Collabora, OnlyOffice No Collabora, OnlyOffice No 
 Database MariaDB or PostgreSQL None Yes, for metadata None See docs See docs 
 Documented minimum 128 MB RAM per PHP process 512 MB RAM (up to 10 users) 2 cores, 2 GB RAM Runs on desktops and phones See docs Small 
 License AGPL-3.0 Apache 2.0 AGPL-3.0 / Apache 2.0 MPL-2.0 AGPL-3.0 Apache 2.0 
 How to run them
 The usual way is on your own server with Docker. All of these projects publish Docker images or a Docker Compose setup, and a small VPS or a home server is enough for most of them. You then look after updates, backups and HTTPS yourself. For a file cloud, backups matter more than anything else: a sync tool happily syncs a deletion to every device.
 If you'd rather not run a server, a managed host takes that part off your hands. On blitz.cloud Ad , Nextcloud, OpenCloud Ad , Syncthing Ad and FileBrowser Quantum Ad install in one click from its App Store, hosted in the EU with HTTPS included. There is a free plan without a credit card, where apps sleep after 30 minutes without visitors. That is fine for trying things out, less so for a sync server your phone talks to all day.
 New to running your own apps? Start with self-hosting for beginners . For photo backup specifically, see Google Photos alternatives . For a closer look at the three main contenders, read Nextcloud vs OpenCloud vs Seafile , and the full list lives under Dropbox alternatives .
 FAQ
 What is the best free Dropbox alternative?
 For most people Nextcloud, because it covers sync, sharing, mobile photo upload and office editing in one place. If you only need files and want a lighter server, try OpenCloud. If you don't want a server at all, use Syncthing.
 Can I self-host Dropbox?
 No, Dropbox is not available for self-hosting. The tools in this guide replace it with software you run yourself.
 Is Syncthing a replacement for Dropbox?
 For syncing your own devices, yes. It has no share links and no web file view, so it does not replace Dropbox for sending files to other people.
 Which one runs on a Raspberry Pi?
 OpenCloud documents a Raspberry Pi 3 class machine for up to 10 users. Syncthing runs on almost anything. Nextcloud works on a Pi too, but it gets slow once you add office editing and several users.
 What happened to File Browser?
 The original File Browser project was archived on 1 September 2026 and gets no more bug or security fixes. FileBrowser Quantum is an actively developed fork.

Best Self-Hosted File Sync & Storage in 2026 | selfhosting.sh 
 Quick Picks
 Use Case Best Choice Why 
 Best overall Nextcloud Full cloud platform — file sync, calendar, contacts, office docs, 400+ apps 
 Best pure file sync Seafile Block-level dedup makes it the fastest sync engine available 
 Best peer-to-peer Syncthing No central server, no account, no trust required 
 Best lightweight platform ownCloud oCIS Single container, no database, Spaces for teams 
 Best lightweight file manager Filebrowser Web UI for server files in 20 MB of RAM 
 Best Dropbox replacement Seafile Closest experience to Dropbox’s fast, reliable sync 
 Best Google Drive replacement Nextcloud File sync + collaborative editing + office suite 
 Get the Docker Compose configs, hardware picks, and setup shortcuts we don’t put in articles. Weekly. No spam.
 The Full Ranking
 1. Nextcloud — Best Overall
 Nextcloud is the Swiss Army knife of self-hosted cloud platforms. File sync and sharing is just the starting point — it includes calendar, contacts, talk (video calls), office document editing (via Collabora or OnlyOffice), notes, tasks, and a plugin ecosystem with 400+ apps. If you want one platform to replace Google Workspace or Microsoft 365, Nextcloud is it.
 The trade-off is resource usage. Nextcloud is a PHP application backed by PostgreSQL and Redis, and it needs 2-4 GB of RAM to run comfortably. Its sync client is slower than Seafile’s because it operates on whole files rather than block-level chunks. Large file libraries (100K+ files) can make the sync client sluggish.
 Pros: 
 Complete cloud platform — files, calendar, contacts, office docs, video calls
 400+ apps in the Nextcloud App Store
 Desktop and mobile sync clients for every platform
 Collaborative document editing with Collabora or OnlyOffice integration
 Massive community (27K+ GitHub stars), extensive documentation
 LDAP/AD integration, SSO, and granular sharing permissions
 End-to-end encryption for sensitive folders
 Cons: 
 Higher resource usage (2-4 GB RAM recommended)
 Sync speed is slower than Seafile for large libraries
 PHP stack requires more tuning for performance (opcache, APCu, cron)
 Upgrades can break apps — test before updating
 Admin UI is sprawling — many settings spread across multiple pages
 Best for: Anyone who wants a single platform replacing Dropbox, Google Drive, Google Calendar, Google Contacts, and Google Docs. The all-in-one play.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Nextcloud 
 2. Seafile — Best Pure File Sync
 Seafile does one thing exceptionally well: sync files fast and reliably. Its custom data model uses block-level deduplication, meaning only changed portions of files are transferred — not entire files. This makes Seafile noticeably faster than Nextcloud for large file operations and repositories with thousands of files.
 Seafile provides file versioning, client-side encryption for libraries, and collaborative editing via SeaDoc. It lacks the app ecosystem of Nextcloud (no calendar, contacts, or plugins), but that focus is also its strength — fewer moving parts, fewer things to break, and lower resource consumption.
 Pros: 
 Fastest sync engine of any self-hosted solution (block-level dedup)
 Client-side encrypted libraries — the server never sees plaintext
 Lower resource usage than Nextcloud (1-2 GB RAM)
 Desktop and mobile sync clients for all platforms
 File versioning and snapshots
 Stable — fewer upgrade issues than Nextcloud
 Active development since 2012
 Cons: 
 No app ecosystem — file sync and sharing only
 No calendar, contacts, or office suite
 Community Edition has limited features vs. Pro
 Fewer integrations than Nextcloud
 Smaller community than Nextcloud (12K GitHub stars)
 Best for: Users who want Dropbox-like file sync without the bloat. If you only need file sync and don’t care about calendar, contacts, or office docs, Seafile is the better choice over Nextcloud.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Seafile 
 3. Syncthing — Best Peer-to-Peer
 Syncthing is fundamentally different from Nextcloud and Seafile. There is no central server. Your devices sync directly with each other over encrypted connections. No account, no cloud, no single point of failure. If one device goes offline, the others keep syncing between themselves.
 This architecture makes Syncthing the most private option — your data never touches a server you don’t control. It also means zero server maintenance for the sync itself. The Docker setup is optional; Syncthing runs natively on Linux, macOS, Windows, and Android.
 The downside: no web UI for file browsing (just the admin dashboard), no link-based sharing, and no mobile file access unless the device with the files is online and running Syncthing.
 Pros: 
 No central server required — true peer-to-peer
 Encrypted in transit, optional encryption at rest
 Works on Linux, macOS, Windows, Android, FreeBSD
 Extremely lightweight (~50 MB RAM)
 No account needed — device IDs handle trust
 67K+ GitHub stars — massive, active community
 Conflict handling with .sync-conflict files
 Cons: 
 No web-based file access or sharing links
 No mobile file browsing (iOS app is limited)
 Requires at least two devices to be useful
 No file versioning beyond simple conflict copies
 No collaborative editing
 Folder sharing requires manual device pairing on both ends
 Best for: Privacy-focused users who want file sync between devices without trusting any server. Pairs well with a Nextcloud or Filebrowser instance for web access.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Syncthing 
 4. ownCloud oCIS — Best Lightweight Platform
 ownCloud oCIS is a complete rewrite of ownCloud in Go. It runs as a single container with no external database — metadata is stored in the filesystem. Spaces (project-based collaboration areas) are a standout feature that Nextcloud doesn’t natively offer. Lighter and faster than Nextcloud, with a modern web UI.
 Pros: 
 Single container — no database, cache, or cron needed
 Lower resource usage than Nextcloud (256-512 MB RAM)
 Spaces for project-based team collaboration
 Built-in identity provider and OIDC support
 Fast startup (compiled Go binary)
 Apache-2.0 license
 Cons: 
 No CalDAV/CardDAV (no calendar or contacts)
 No video calls or app marketplace
 Smaller community and less documentation than Nextcloud
 Enterprise-focused — fewer community tutorials
 Legacy ownCloud 10 (PHP) is a different product in maintenance mode
 Best for: Teams who want file sync with project-based collaboration (Spaces) and prefer a lighter, simpler platform than Nextcloud.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host ownCloud oCIS 
 5. Filebrowser — Best Lightweight File Manager
 Filebrowser is not a sync tool. It is a web-based file manager that gives you browser access to files on your server. Upload, download, rename, move, share via link — all through a clean web UI. It runs in ~20 MB of RAM with a single container.
 Filebrowser fills a different niche than the sync tools above. Use it when you want web access to files on a server without installing sync clients on every device. It supports multiple users with configurable permissions, link-based sharing with optional passwords and expiry, and a built-in text editor.
 Pros: 
 Extremely lightweight (~20 MB RAM, single container)
 Clean, fast web UI
 Multi-user with per-user root directories and permissions
 Link-based file sharing with passwords and expiry
 Built-in text/code editor
 Zero configuration to get started
 Cons: 
 No sync client — web only
 No file versioning
 No mobile app
 No calendar, contacts, or collaboration features
 Limited to what a web file manager can do
 Best for: Accessing server files from a browser. Use alongside Syncthing for sync + web access, or as a lightweight alternative when Nextcloud is overkill.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Filebrowser 
 Full Comparison Table
 Feature Nextcloud Seafile Syncthing Filebrowser 
 Architecture Client-server Client-server Peer-to-peer Web file manager 
 Desktop sync client Yes Yes Yes No 
 Mobile sync client Yes (Android, iOS) Yes (Android, iOS) Yes (Android; limited iOS) No 
 Web file browser Yes Yes No (admin UI only) Yes 
 Link-based sharing Yes Yes No Yes 
 File versioning Yes Yes (snapshots) No No 
 Client-side encryption Per-folder E2E Per-library In transit No 
 Collaborative editing Yes (Collabora/OnlyOffice) Yes (SeaDoc) No No 
 Calendar & contacts Yes No No No 
 App ecosystem 400+ plugins Limited None None 
 Multi-user Yes Yes N/A (device-based) Yes 
 LDAP/SSO Yes Yes (Pro) No No 
 RAM usage (idle) 500-800 MB 300-500 MB ~50 MB ~20 MB 
 Containers required 3+ (app, db, Redis) 3 (server, db, memcached) 1 1 
 Sync speed (large files) Moderate Fast (block-level) Fast (direct) N/A 
 GitHub stars 27K+ 12K+ 67K+ 27K+ 
 License AGPL-3.0 AGPL-3.0 MPL-2.0 Apache-2.0 
 How We Evaluated
 Each solution was assessed on six criteria:
 Sync reliability and speed — How fast does it sync large files and large numbers of files? Does it handle conflicts cleanly?
 Resource efficiency — RAM, CPU, and disk overhead on the server. Matters for small home servers and VPS instances.
 Feature breadth — What can you do beyond basic file sync? Sharing, versioning, encryption, collaboration.
 Setup complexity — How many containers, how much configuration, how quickly can you go from zero to working?
 Client coverage — Desktop and mobile app availability, browser access, API quality.
 Community and maintenance — GitHub activity, documentation quality, release cadence, community size.
 Nextcloud wins overall because it replaces the most cloud services in a single deployment. Seafile wins for pure sync because its block-level engine is measurably faster. Syncthing wins for privacy because no data ever touches a central server. Filebrowser wins for simplicity when you just need web file access without sync overhead.
 FAQ
 Can I use Syncthing and Nextcloud together?
 Yes, and it is a common setup. Use Syncthing for fast device-to-device sync of working files, and Nextcloud for web access, sharing links, calendar, and contacts. They serve different purposes and complement each other well. Just avoid syncing the same directory with both tools simultaneously — pick one sync engine per folder.
 Which is the best Dropbox replacement?
 Seafile. Its block-level sync engine is the closest experience to Dropbox in terms of speed and reliability. Nextcloud is the better choice if you also want to replace Google Calendar, Contacts, and Docs alongside Dropbox.
 How much storage do I need?
 As much as you have files. All four solutions store data on your server’s filesystem. Start with whatever disk space you have and expand with additional drives, NAS, or network mounts. For reference, the average Dropbox user stores 2-5 GB — most home servers have far more than that available.
 Do I need a reverse proxy for these?
 For remote access with HTTPS, yes. All four work behind Nginx Proxy Manager, Traefik, or Caddy . Syncthing is the exception for sync traffic (it handles its own encryption), but the web UI benefits from a reverse proxy if exposed remotely.

Best Open Source Alternatives to Dropbox in 2026 — OSSAlt Guides | OSSAlt 
 Skip to main content Contents Dropbox Keeps Getting More Expensive 
 Dropbox Plus costs $11.99/month for 2 TB. Professional runs $19.99/month (annual) or $24.99 monthly for 3 TB. Business starts at $18/user/month for teams.
 For a 20-person team on Business, that's $4,320 per year — for file sync and sharing. And you're still capped on storage, locked into Dropbox's ecosystem, and trusting a third party with every file your organization creates.
 Dropbox scans file contents for "abuse detection" and shares metadata with third-party analytics providers. Their privacy policy permits training AI models on your data unless you opt out — and opting out requires an Enterprise plan.
 Open source file sync tools give you the same core functionality — sync across devices, file sharing, versioning — running on your own hardware with no storage caps and no third-party access to your files. Here are the best options in 2026.
 TL;DR 
 Nextcloud is the best overall Dropbox replacement if you want a full platform — file sync plus office suite, calendar, contacts, chat, and more (see our guide to migrating from Dropbox to Nextcloud for a step-by-step walkthrough). If you only need file sync with zero server infrastructure, Syncthing is the most elegant solution with peer-to-peer encrypted sync and no central server required. For teams that handle large files and need raw sync speed, Seafile is the fastest option.
 Key Takeaways 
 Nextcloud (34K+ stars) is the most complete alternative — files, office docs, calendar, chat, video calls — but the breadth creates complexity and performance overhead.
 Syncthing (78K+ stars) is peer-to-peer with no server needed, fully encrypted, and truly decentralized. It does one thing exceptionally well: sync files between devices.
 Seafile (14K+ stars) uses block-level deduplication for fast sync performance, especially with large files. The leanest server-based option.
 ownCloud rewrote their stack in Go (OCIS) for better performance and simpler deployment. Enterprise-focused with strong compliance features.
 FileRun offers the most polished web-based file manager with a Dropbox-like UI, but it's not fully open source — free for up to 5 users, paid enterprise beyond that.
 Self-hosting file sync saves money starting around 5-10 users because storage costs scale linearly on Dropbox but stay flat on your own server.
 Storage is the key differentiator: Dropbox caps you at 2-3 TB per user. Self-hosted solutions use as much disk as you attach.
 Quick Comparison 
 Tool GitHub Stars Server Required Sync Speed Mobile Apps File Versioning Office Integration License 
 Nextcloud 34.3K Yes Moderate iOS + Android Yes Collabora/OnlyOffice AGPL-3.0 
 Syncthing 78K+ No (P2P) Fast Android (community iOS) File-level No MPL-2.0 
 Seafile 14.3K Yes Very Fast iOS + Android Yes (snapshots) OnlyOffice/Collabora AGPL-3.0 
 ownCloud OCIS 1.8K Yes Fast iOS + Android Yes Collabora/OnlyOffice Apache-2.0 
 FileRun N/A (proprietary) Yes Fast WebDAV clients Yes Collabora/OnlyOffice Proprietary 
 Nextcloud — Most Complete Dropbox Replacement 
 Nextcloud is a full collaboration platform that happens to include file sync. You get cloud storage, office editing, calendar, contacts, chat, video conferencing, and an app store with hundreds of extensions — all self-hosted.
 Nextcloud 33 (Hub 26), released February 2026, ships with two-factor authentication enabled by default and improved sync performance.
 What It Does Well 
 Breadth of features. Replace Dropbox, Google Calendar, Slack, and Google Docs in one move. Nextcloud Office (Collabora or OnlyOffice) provides real-time collaborative document editing. Nextcloud Talk handles video calls and chat.
 Sharing and collaboration. Share via links with passwords, expiry dates, and download limits. Granular permissions — read-only, upload-only, edit access — mirror what teams expect from Dropbox Business.
 Mobile apps. Official iOS and Android apps handle automatic photo uploads, offline file access, and background sync.
 Federation. Two companies running their own Nextcloud instances can share folders server-to-server — something Dropbox can't do.
 Self-Hosting Requirements 
 Nextcloud server — PHP application (Apache or Nginx)
 PostgreSQL or MySQL/MariaDB — database
 Redis — caching (strongly recommended)
 The Nextcloud All-in-One Docker image manages the full stack — automatic updates, backups, and SSL in one container. Minimum hardware: 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM for under 20 users. Our Nextcloud self-hosting guide covers the full setup including storage configuration and SSL.
 Limitations 
 Performance is Nextcloud's persistent weakness. The PHP stack feels sluggish compared to Dropbox during large syncs. The desktop client still lags behind Seafile in raw throughput. And the scope of features creates maintenance overhead — if you only need file sync, Nextcloud is overkill.
 Best for: Teams that want to replace Dropbox and several other cloud services with a single self-hosted platform.
 Syncthing — Best for Decentralized, Serverless Sync 
 There's no server. No cloud. No account. Files sync directly between your devices using encrypted peer-to-peer connections.
 Syncthing v2, released February 2026, uses multiple simultaneous connections by default (one for metadata, two for data transfer), structured logging, and automatic cleanup of deleted items after fifteen months.
 What It Does Well 
 Zero infrastructure. Install on two or more devices, connect them, choose folders to sync. No server, no database, no SSL certificates. Files travel directly between machines, encrypted with TLS.
 Privacy by design. Data never touches a third-party server. Relay servers are used only when direct connections fail, and all relay traffic is end-to-end encrypted — relays can't read your files.
 Smart conflict handling. Syncthing preserves both versions of conflicting files rather than silently overwriting. Block-based sync transfers only changed portions, making it efficient for large files.
 Cross-platform. Windows, macOS, Linux, Android, FreeBSD. Every device is a peer — a laptop, desktop, phone, and NAS can all sync different subsets with different peers. LAN devices sync locally without internet traffic.
 Limitations 
 No web interface for files. No browser-based file manager, no shareable download links. If you need web access or link sharing, Syncthing isn't the tool.
 No central storage. Without a dedicated always-on device (NAS or VPS) as a persistent peer, files only exist on powered-on devices.
 iOS is community-maintained. Official Android app exists, but iOS relies on third-party apps like Mobius Sync.
 No collaboration. No permissions, no comments, no office integration. Syncthing syncs files — nothing more.
 Best for: Individuals and small groups who want private, serverless file sync without depending on any third party.
 Seafile — Fastest Sync for Large Files 
 Seafile focuses on one thing: fast, reliable file synchronization. No platform bloat — just the best sync engine with a clean web interface. Seafile 9.0.5 shipped in February 2026 with improved error handling and file monitoring fixes.
 What It Does Well 
 Sync speed. Seafile consistently benchmarks as the fastest self-hosted sync solution. Block-level deduplication splits files into blocks and only transfers changed blocks. For large files that change frequently (video, design, databases), this is dramatically faster than re-uploading entire files.
 Storage efficiency. Identical content across files is stored once. Fifty copies of the same PDF across users' folders? Seafile stores the blocks once, cutting storage requirements by 30-50% for teams with significant overlap.
 Client-side encryption. Libraries (Seafile's file containers) can be encrypted with a password the server never sees — true zero-knowledge encryption. Dropbox doesn't offer anything comparable.
 Lightweight web UI. File browsing, link sharing, inline previews, and a Markdown editor. Fast and responsive because it doesn't try to do everything.
 Self-Hosting Requirements 
 Seafile server — core sync engine (C/Python)
 MariaDB/MySQL — database
 Memcached — caching (optional)
 Runs on a VPS with 1 GB of RAM. Community Edition is free for unlimited users. Professional Edition (free for up to 3 users) adds full-text search, LDAP sync, and audit logging.
 Limitations 
 No plugin ecosystem. No calendar, contacts, or chat. Office integration (Collabora/OnlyOffice) requires separate setup.
 Library-based model. Files must belong to a library — you can't sync arbitrary filesystem folders like Dropbox or Syncthing.
 Dated mobile apps. iOS and Android apps work but lack the polish of Nextcloud's or Dropbox's mobile clients.
 Best for: Teams that prioritize sync speed and storage efficiency, especially with large files.
 ownCloud OCIS — Enterprise-Grade Rewrite in Go 
 ownCloud was the original self-hosted cloud storage project (Nextcloud forked from it in 2016). OCIS (Infinite Scale) is a complete rewrite in Go — single binary, no PHP, no external database required. OCIS 8.0.0, released February 2026, added brute-force protection for public links and multi-instance sharing.
 What It Does Well 
 Single binary deployment. Download one Go binary, run it, and you have a file sync server. No PHP runtime, no database install, no web server configuration. The simplest deployment of any server-based option on this list.
 Performance. The Go rewrite is noticeably faster than PHP-based ownCloud 10 and competes well with Nextcloud on response times.
 Spaces. Shared project workspaces with their own quotas, permissions, and members — maps better to how teams organize files than traditional folder hierarchies.
 Enterprise compliance. Full audit logging, GDPR tools, LDAP/AD integration, and granular sharing policies.
 Self-Hosting Requirements 
 OCIS binary — single application or Docker image
 No external database required (built-in storage)
 No web server needed (built-in HTTP server)
 Add a reverse proxy for SSL in production. But for getting started, it's one binary.
 Limitations 
 Smaller community. 1.8K GitHub stars versus Nextcloud's 34K. Fewer third-party resources and community support.
 Kiteworks acquisition. ownCloud's acquisition adds enterprise stability but raises open source direction questions. Core is Apache-2.0 licensed.
 Fewer integrations. No calendar, contacts, or chat built in. OCIS is focused on files and document collaboration.
 Best for: Organizations that want performant file sync with enterprise compliance and minimal deployment complexity.
 FileRun — Most Polished Web File Manager 
 FileRun is the odd one out — it's proprietary, not open source. But its web interface is the closest to Dropbox's polished UX that you can self-host. Free for up to 5 users, paid enterprise beyond that. FileRun 2026.1.0 shipped with faster ZIP downloads, optimized WebDAV, and Nextcloud favorites compatibility.
 What It Does Well 
 User experience. Clean, fast web interface with drag-and-drop uploads, inline previews for images/videos/PDFs/office docs, and a file manager that feels like a native app. Lowest learning curve for non-technical users.
 WebDAV sync. No proprietary sync client — uses standard WebDAV, so any compatible client works. Mount as a network drive on macOS/Windows natively.
 Access control. Per-user and per-folder permissions, guest accounts, and the ability to disable specific access methods (API, WebDAV, desktop) per user.
 Media handling. Thumbnail generation, EXIF extraction, video streaming, music playback. Good for teams using Dropbox as a media library.
 Self-Hosting Requirements 
 FileRun application — PHP-based web app
 MariaDB/MySQL — database
 Nginx or Apache — web server
 Standard LAMP deployment with Docker images available. Light resource footprint.
 Limitations 
 Not open source. Proprietary with a free tier (up to 5 users). Doesn't qualify for strictly open source evaluations.
 No native sync client. WebDAV works but lacks Dropbox-level sync polish — conflict resolution depends on your chosen client.
 Limited collaboration. File manager only — no built-in office editing, comments, or real-time collaboration.
 Best for: Small teams (under 5 users) who want the most polished self-hosted file management UI.
 How to Choose 
 "I want to replace Dropbox and Google Workspace together" — Nextcloud . Files, docs, calendar, contacts, chat, and video calls in one platform. Accept the complexity.
 "I just want my files synced between my devices, no server" — Syncthing . Install it, pair your devices, forget about it. Private, serverless, zero maintenance.
 "I work with large files and sync speed matters" — Seafile . Block-level dedup and the fastest sync engine in the group. Especially good for video, design, and engineering teams.
 "I need the simplest possible server deployment" — ownCloud OCIS . One binary, no database required. Running in minutes.
 "My users aren't technical and need a familiar UI" — FileRun (free for up to 5 users). The closest thing to Dropbox's interface you can self-host.
 "I need compliance and enterprise features" — ownCloud OCIS or Nextcloud Enterprise . Both offer audit logging, LDAP integration, and compliance tooling. ownCloud's enterprise heritage gives it a slight edge in regulated environments.
 Cost Comparison: Dropbox vs Self-Hosting 
 For a 20-person team, Dropbox costs $4,320-$7,200/year depending on your plan. Storage-heavy teams pay even more. Here's what self-hosting looks like.

 The key difference is storage scaling . On Dropbox, more storage means higher plans. Self-hosted, you add a $50-$100 hard drive. At 10+ TB, the cost gap becomes massive.
 Syncthing eliminates server costs entirely — each person uses their own device storage plus an optional NAS ($200-$500 one-time) as a persistent peer. If you already have server infrastructure , adding Seafile or Nextcloud is near-zero marginal cost. Teams that want to go further with server-side data protection should read our guide to automated server backups with restic and rclone .
 Methodology 
 We evaluated these tools based on:
 Sync reliability and speed — File transfer performance, conflict handling, delta sync, and behavior with large file trees.
 Self-hosting viability — Deployment complexity, resource requirements, documentation quality, and operational overhead.
 Feature parity with Dropbox — File sharing, link sharing, mobile auto-upload, file versioning, search, and collaboration.
 Community health — GitHub stars, commit frequency, release cadence, and community support as of March 2026.
 Privacy and security — Encryption options (at-rest, in-transit, client-side), data access policies, and telemetry.
 We did not accept payment or sponsorship from any project listed. Tools were tested via self-hosted deployments (Docker or native) where available.

 A NAS is more than backup storage. These 8 self-hosted apps run 24/7 on Synology, Unraid, and TrueNAS to replace paid subscriptions with local services.

 The XDA piece on NAS owners who only use their box for a nightly 3am backup nailed the missed opportunity. The drives are spinning, the CPU is idle, the network stack is warm. A modern NAS is the only always-on Linux machine most households have, and its real payoff shows up when it hosts the services people would otherwise pay a monthly bill for. Once Docker is wired up (via Synology Container Manager, TrueNAS apps, Unraid Community Applications, or plain docker-compose on a mini-PC), the subscription savings pile up quickly.
 We tested 8 apps that run 24/7 on Synology, Unraid, and TrueNAS to replace paid subscriptions with local services. The lineup covers personal cloud (Nextcloud), photo backup (Immich), media streaming (Jellyfin), DNS-level ad blocking (Pi-hole), smart-home automation (Home Assistant), passwords (Vaultwarden), documents (Paperless-ngx), and self-monitoring (Uptime Kuma). Every pick ships as a maintained Docker image, sits well below 1GB of idle RAM, and has a mobile client the rest of the household can actually use.
 What to look for in a 24/7 NAS app
 Not every self-hosted project earns a permanent slot on an appliance that stays powered on all year. The ones that do share a few traits:
 A first-party Docker image with a versioned tag and a :latest that the maintainers actually push. If the container comes from a stranger’s personal Docker Hub account, skip it.
 Active maintenance in the last 90 days. Check the GitHub commit graph before you commit to migrating a family off a paid service.
 An idle RAM footprint you can budget. Under 512MB is the mark; anything that idles at 2GB will crowd out the other services.
 A mobile client that the rest of the household will accept. Nobody in the family will SSH into your NAS to check something.
 Named Docker volumes and a documented backup procedure. Container-native persistence is the difference between a hobby project and a service you can rely on.
 Reverse-proxy friendliness. Traefik, Caddy, or NGINX Proxy Manager should be able to sit in front without a config battle, because remote access needs TLS.

 The 8 best apps to run 24/7 on a NAS
 1. Nextcloud – best replacement for Dropbox and Google Drive
 Nextcloud is where most self-hosted setups start. It handles file sync, calendars, contacts, notes, and lightweight collaborative editing through the Nextcloud Office app. Desktop clients cover Windows, macOS, and Linux with selective sync, and the mobile apps auto-upload the camera roll on iOS and Android. A NAS with 4GB of RAM comfortably serves a family of four.
 Where it falls short: Out-of-the-box performance needs the recommended PHP-FPM, Redis, and OPcache tuning to feel snappy under load. External sharing links behind a reverse proxy require careful trusted_domains and overwrite.cli.url config.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source (AGPLv3)
 Nextcloud Enterprise support contracts available for organisations
 Platforms: Linux, Docker, Synology (SynoCommunity package), TrueNAS Scale apps catalogue, Unraid Community Applications. Native desktop clients on Windows, macOS, Linux. Mobile clients on iOS and Android.
 Download: Nextcloud 
 Bottom line: The default cloud replacement if you want to keep the whole household off Google Drive and Dropbox.
 2. Immich – best replacement for Google Photos
 Immich is the photo-and-video backup service that finally makes leaving Google Photos comfortable. Face recognition, object search, geolocation maps, shared albums, and background upload from iOS and Android all work out of the box. The machine-learning worker runs happily on ARM as well as x86, so a Synology DS923+ or a TrueNAS Mini can index a decade of camera roll without help from a GPU.
 Where it falls short: Version numbers move fast, so a mobile client that gets ahead of the server (or the other way around) breaks uploads until you catch up. The maintainers still label the project as beta even though thousands of installs run it in production.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source (AGPLv3)
 Platforms: Linux, Docker. Mobile clients on iOS and Android. Browser interface for desktops.
 Download: Immich 
 Bottom line: The 2026 pick for anyone tired of paying Google for photo storage.
 3. Jellyfin – best free media server for the whole house
 Jellyfin is the open-source media server that took over from Plex for anyone who wanted to skip Plex Pass and the recent pricing shuffles. Hardware transcoding runs on Intel Quick Sync, Nvidia NVENC, and AMD VAAPI, and the client app coverage spans iOS, Android, Apple TV, Android TV, Roku, Fire TV, and LG webOS. No cloud sign-in, no Plex account, no telemetry surprises.
 Where it falls short: First-run library scanning takes a while, and metadata cleanup rewards a bit of manual work. Dolby Vision Profile 7 and Atmos passthrough still need per-client configuration on a couple of platforms.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Platforms: Linux, Docker, Windows, macOS. Native TV clients on every major platform.
 Download: Jellyfin 
 Bottom line: The pick if the household streams enough that Netflix, Disney+, and Max add up faster than the disk cost.
 4. Pi-hole – best network-wide DNS ad blocker
 Pi-hole turns the NAS into the DNS server for every device on the network. Smart TVs, IoT cameras, phones, and the kid’s Switch all resolve through it, and the tracker and ad blocklists apply transparently without per-device installs. The web UI shows per-client query breakdowns and blocklist hit rates in real time. Upstream DoH via cloudflared or Unbound is a standard add-on.
 Where it falls short: YouTube ads served from the same origin as the video stream are a moving target, and DNS-level blocking does not catch them. A Pi-hole that goes offline knocks out name resolution for the whole network, so redundancy or a secondary DNS matters.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Platforms: Linux, Docker, Raspberry Pi. Synology and QNAP packages ship via Docker.
 Download: Pi-hole 
 Bottom line: The pick if you want every device in the house to feel faster without touching each one.
 5. Home Assistant – best local smart home hub
 Home Assistant is the automation platform that runs the smart-home stack locally rather than through a vendor cloud. The integration catalogue crossed 2,000 in 2025 and covers Zigbee, Z-Wave, Matter, Thread, MQTT, and every mainstream vendor API. Automations run in YAML or in the graphical editor, and voice control ties in via the Assist pipeline. Runs on Docker, on the dedicated HA OS image, or through a Synology community package.
 Where it falls short: The learning curve is real, especially the difference between the OS install and the Container install for what add-ons will and will not run. Cloud-only devices (some Wi-Fi cameras, first-gen smart plugs) still need vendor apps or Nabu Casa in the middle.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Optional Nabu Casa cloud subscription (around $6.50/month) for remote access, Alexa, and Google Assistant integration
 Platforms: Linux, Docker, dedicated HA OS on x86 or Raspberry Pi. Mobile apps on iOS and Android.
 Download: Home Assistant 
 Bottom line: The pick if you want smart-home automation to keep working the day a vendor cloud goes down.
 6. Vaultwarden – best self-hosted password manager
 Vaultwarden is the Rust-based Bitwarden server rewrite that fits happily on a NAS. It speaks the full Bitwarden client protocol, so the official iOS, Android, browser, and desktop apps all connect to it. Idle RAM sits under 50MB, and storage requirements measure in megabytes. Family sharing, TOTP generation, attachment storage, and organisation features all work as they do on Bitwarden’s hosted plan.
 Where it falls short: The upstream Bitwarden company does not maintain Vaultwarden, so major protocol changes occasionally take a release cycle to land. Bootstrapping the reverse proxy and TLS correctly matters more here than for any other app on this list.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Platforms: Linux, Docker. Every Bitwarden client on iOS, Android, browser, Windows, macOS, and Linux connects to it.
 Download: Vaultwarden 
 Bottom line: The pick if you want the Bitwarden client experience without paying the yearly family plan fee.
 7. Paperless-ngx – best document archive
 Paperless-ngx turns a NAS into the searchable archive for every bill, tax return, medical record, and warranty PDF that used to live in a filing cabinet. Drop a scanned PDF into a watched folder and the OCR pipeline extracts text, tags by correspondent and document type, and files it against the year. Search across years of documents takes under a second once the index is built. Full-text search works in every language the Tesseract data pack supports.
 Where it falls short: The consumption folder workflow needs a working network scanner setup, and the initial rule tuning pays off long-term. First-run OCR on a large backlog is CPU-heavy for a few hours.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Platforms: Linux, Docker. Ships in the Synology, Unraid, and TrueNAS app catalogues. Mobile apps (Paperless Mobile on Android, Paperless Share on iOS) round out the workflow.
 Download: Paperless-ngx 
 Bottom line: The pick if there is a physical filing cabinet you would like to retire this year.
 8. Uptime Kuma – best self-hosted uptime monitor
 Uptime Kuma is the local answer to Uptime Robot and Pingdom. Point it at the URLs, ports, DNS records, and Docker containers you care about, and it pings them on your schedule. Notifications route to email, Discord, Slack, ntfy, Telegram, and roughly ninety other channels. Public status pages ship in the same install, so a household that shares Jellyfin and Nextcloud can see at a glance whether the NAS is reachable.
 Where it falls short: Distributed monitoring across geographic regions needs a second Uptime Kuma running elsewhere or a paid third-party service. The status pages are functional rather than polished.
 Pricing: 
 Free, open-source
 Platforms: Linux, Docker.
 Download: Uptime Kuma 
 Bottom line: The pick to install last, so the rest of the stack has a watchdog before the family notices something is down.
 How to pick the right one
 If you want the single biggest subscription saver: Nextcloud plus Immich. Together they cover Dropbox, Google Drive, and Google Photos for the whole household, and the combined bill from the cloud versions is usually enough to justify the NAS on its own.
 If the household budget is the driver: Jellyfin plus Pi-hole. Streaming and network-wide ad blocking with zero recurring cost, and both are visible improvements the rest of the family will notice.
 If smart-home privacy is the reason you bought the NAS: Home Assistant is the anchor. Add Vaultwarden alongside it and you have moved the two most vendor-locked services in the house in-house.
 If the filing cabinet by the desk is the source of stress: Paperless-ngx first. Point a network scanner at the consumption folder, feed it the backlog on a weekend, and the paper problem quietly goes away.
 If you already run three or four of these: Uptime Kuma is the tenth-birthday cake. It watches the rest so you find out about a dead container before anyone else does.
 FAQ
 How much RAM does a NAS need to run all 8? 
Nextcloud is the largest at roughly 512MB after warm-up. Immich reaches 2GB when the machine-learning worker is indexing. Jellyfin peaks around 500MB during a transcode. Everything else sits under 200MB idle. An 8GB NAS handles the full stack with headroom; 16GB is the sweet spot if you also want ZFS with a decent ARC.
 Do these apps work on Synology? 
All eight. Synology’s Container Manager runs the official Docker images for every app on this list. Nextcloud, Vaultwarden, and Home Assistant also have community-maintained native packages via SynoCommunity if you would rather skip Docker for those.
 Do I need Docker to self-host these? 
For seven of the eight, Docker is the path of least resistance. Home Assistant can also run as its own dedicated OS on a small mini-PC or Raspberry Pi with a wider add-on catalogue. Everything else is easier to update, back up, and roll back when it lives in a container with a named volume.
 How do you back up the self-hosted services themselves? 
Snapshot the app-data directory nightly, replicate it off-box (to another NAS, a cloud bucket like Backblaze B2, or an external drive on rotation), and test the restore once a quarter. Nextcloud and Vaultwarden both ship documented backup CLI commands worth wiring into a cron job.
 Can these apps really replace Google Photos, Dropbox, and Netflix at the same time? 
Yes, and that is the point of running them together. Nextcloud replaces Dropbox and Google Drive. Immich replaces Google Photos. Jellyfin replaces Netflix and Disney+ for content you already own. Adding Vaultwarden also displaces 1Password or the Bitwarden hosted plan. The combined savings usually cover the NAS drives inside a year.
 Is self-hosting genuinely more private than the cloud versions? 
Only if you set up TLS properly, keep the underlying OS patched, and avoid exposing admin ports to the public internet. Self-hosting shifts the trust boundary from the vendor to your own operational discipline. Fronting everything with a Tailscale or WireGuard tunnel instead of public port forwards is the shortcut that makes the privacy claim genuine.

 A focused file-sync platform that is faster and more reliable at large libraries than Nextcloud.
 Visit Seafile site Runs on Docker, ~1-2 GB RAM 
 Pick it if You want rock-solid, fast sync for lots of files and do not need the extra apps. 
 Syncthing
 MPL, free 
 Peer-to-peer sync with no central server. Devices sync directly to each other.
 Visit Syncthing site Runs on Tiny. Runs on a Pi or any always-on device 
 Pick it if You want device-to-device sync with no server and no cloud, just folders kept in sync. 
 The verdict
 Run Nextcloud if you want a true Dropbox replacement with sharing and apps. Run Seafile if you only need fast, reliable file sync and want it to stay out of the way. Run Syncthing if you do not want a central server at all and just need folders mirrored between your own devices. Many people run Syncthing for personal device sync and Nextcloud for sharing with others.
 FAQ
 What is the best self-hosted Dropbox alternative?
 Nextcloud, if you want files plus sharing, calendar, and apps. Seafile if you want faster, simpler file sync. Syncthing if you want device-to-device sync with no central server.
 Does Nextcloud sync like Dropbox?
 Yes. Nextcloud has sync clients for Windows, Mac, Linux, iOS, and Android that keep folders in sync and let you share files with links, just like Dropbox.
 Is Syncthing a full Dropbox replacement?
 Partly. Syncthing keeps folders in sync directly between your own devices with no server and no cloud, but it has no share-by-link or web access. It is great for personal device sync, less so for sharing with others.

Backup storage 
 Taking backups or pulling a copy
 The NAS takes backups The NAS pulls a copy 
 Where backups land first On the NAS In cloud storage, then on the NAS 
 Router changes A forwarded port or a tunnel None 
 The NAS is reachable from the internet Yes No 
 Copies you end up with One, at home Two, in two places 
 If your home internet is down Backups fail until it is back Backups carry on; the NAS catches up later 
 For most people pulling is the better choice. It keeps the cloud copy, adds a second one at home, and never exposes the NAS. It is the 3-2-1 rule with the NAS as the second copy.
 Taking backups directly makes sense when the NAS is the only storage you want to pay for, and you are prepared to keep it patched and reachable.
 QNAP
 QNAP's free QuObjects app turns a shared folder into S3-compatible storage: buckets, presigned URLs and multipart uploads, which is what backup tools use. It runs on every x86 QNAP and on the ARM models in the TS-x32 series and the TS-1635AX, with QTS 5.0.0 or later. Any tool that writes to S3 can then write to the NAS. See how to set up QuObjects for backups .
 To pull instead, Hybrid Backup Sync 3 (HBS 3) has active sync jobs, which copy from a cloud storage space to the NAS. QNAP itself suggests this for a 3-2-1 setup: back up to the cloud, then copy the cloud backup to the NAS. See how to keep a copy on a NAS .
 Synology
 DSM has no S3 server of its own. Synology C2 Object Storage is Synology's cloud service, not something that runs on your NAS. A Synology can still take backups as files: DSM has an rsync service and SFTP, so a server can push with rsync over SSH if the NAS is reachable.
 Pulling is better supported. Cloud Sync connects to S3 storage and has a one-way mode that downloads remote changes only, so the NAS keeps a copy of a bucket without ever uploading to it.
 Cloud Sync downloads a whole file again whenever it changes, even if only part of it did. Backup archives are written once and never changed, so this costs nothing for them, but keep the task's local folder for backups alone.
 UniFi UNAS
 Ubiquiti's UNAS devices run UniFi Drive. It shares files over SMB and backs the NAS up outwards, to another UNAS, an SMB share, or cloud storage such as Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, Amazon S3, Backblaze B2 and Wasabi. It runs no third-party apps or containers, so there is no S3 server to install and no way for the UNAS itself to download from a bucket.
 To get server backups onto a UNAS, let another machine on your network do the pulling. Mount a UNAS share on a computer that is on most of the time, and copy the bucket into it with rclone on a schedule:
 Terminal (a Linux computer on the same network) Copy sudo mkdir -p /mnt/unas
sudo mount -t cifs //192.168.1.20/ServerBackups /mnt/unas -o username=backup,uid=$(id -u)
rclone config create backups s3 provider=AWS region=us-east-1 \
 access_key_id=AKIA... secret_access_key=...
rclone copy backups:my-backup-bucket /mnt/unas --checksum --transfers 4 
 Use a key that can only read the bucket. The machine doing the copying never needs to write to cloud storage.
 Drobo
 Drobo stopped selling its products and supporting them on January 27, 2023, and its parent company, StorCentric, moved to Chapter 7 liquidation in May 2023. There are no more firmware or security updates.
 Don't buy a Drobo for backups, and don't make an existing one reachable from the internet. If one holds data you care about, copy it to supported storage while the unit still works, and keep using it, if at all, only as an extra copy on your home network.
 Before you open a NAS to the internet
 NAS devices reachable from the internet have been targets of ransomware that encrypts everything on them. If the NAS is to take backups directly:
 Expose only the one service backups need, such as QuObjects' port, never the NAS's sign-in page. 
 Prefer a tunnel (Cloudflare Tunnel, for example) to a forwarded port: nothing on your router is opened, and your home address stays hidden. 
 Give backups a user of their own that can reach one shared folder and nothing else. 
 Turn on automatic updates for the operating system and the apps, and turn off services you don't use. 
 Keep another copy somewhere else. A NAS that is encrypted by ransomware takes its backups with it. 
 Frequently asked questions
 Can I use Tailscale to reach my NAS for backups? Only if every machine that uploads is on your tailnet. A backup service running in a data centre cannot reach a Tailscale address, so for a hosted backup tool the NAS needs a public address or a tunnel, or it should pull a copy instead. 
 Is a NAS enough as the only copy of my server backups? Not on its own. It sits in one place, on one power supply and one internet connection. Treat it as one copy of two, with the other in cloud storage. 
 Does a Synology NAS speak S3? Not natively. DSM can download from S3 storage with Cloud Sync and take files over rsync or SFTP, but it has no S3 server of its own.

 Best Dropbox Alternatives for 2026: Free & Premium Tools
 The best Dropbox alternatives are Google Drive for overall collaboration, Sync for privacy-focused teams, Mega for free storage, OneDrive for Microsoft 365 users, and pCloud for lifetime storage plans.
 Written By 
 Faithe Day

 details.
 Dropbox is still a reliable cloud storage and file-sharing tool, but it is no longer the obvious default for every user or business. Its free plan is limited, and many teams now need more specialized features, such as stronger privacy controls, better collaboration tools, deeper Microsoft or Google integration, cloud backup, lifetime storage options, or enterprise-grade file management.
 For most users, Google Drive is the best Dropbox alternative because it offers generous free storage, real-time collaboration, and tight integration with Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Gmail, and Google Workspace. But depending on your needs, another provider may be a better fit:
 Best overall Dropbox alternative: Google Drive 
 Best for privacy-focused teams: Sync 
 Best free storage allowance: Mega 
 Best for Microsoft 365 users: Microsoft OneDrive 
 Best for lifetime storage plans: pCloud 
 Best for cloud backup: IDrive 
 Best for clean interface and virtual drive use: Icedrive 
 Best for businesses and enterprises: Box 
 Best for encrypted file storage: NordLocker 
 Contents
 What is Dropbox? 
 Hidden costs associated with Dropbox 
 Best Dropbox alternatives 
 Methodology: How I evaluated Dropbox alternatives 
 Frequently asked questions (FAQs) 
 What is Dropbox?
 Dropbox is a cloud-based file storage and sharing service that lets users save files in one central location and access them across compatible devices. By adding Dropbox to a desktop, phone, or tablet, users can automatically sync files, share folders with others, back up important documents, and collaborate on work without relying on local storage or email attachments.
 Use the mobile or desktop app to access Dropbox files. (Source: Dropbox) 
 Dropbox is still a strong option for simple file syncing and sharing, but it is no longer the only practical cloud storage choice. Many users now compare Dropbox against tools with more free storage, stronger collaboration features, built-in productivity suites, lifetime storage plans, or privacy-focused encryption.
 Visit Dropbox 
 Hidden costs associated with Dropbox
 Dropbox offers a free Basic plan, but its 2GB storage limit can fill up quickly, even for casual users. That makes it less generous than alternatives like Google Drive, Mega, pCloud, IDrive, and Icedrive, which offer more free storage upfront.
 The first major paid individual plan, Dropbox Plus, increases storage to 2TB for one user and costs $11.99 per month, or $9.99 per month when billed annually. That equals $119.88 per year. This may be reasonable for one person who wants simple syncing and file recovery, but it may not be the best value for users who mainly need free storage, encrypted storage, or access to productivity tools.
 Costs can rise more quickly for teams. Dropbox Standard starts at $15 per user per month when billed annually, includes 5 TB of team storage, and requires at least 3 users. A 10-person team would cost about $1,800 per year before add-ons, higher-tier upgrades, or additional storage needs. Businesses comparing Dropbox alternatives should look beyond storage limits and consider admin controls, security features, collaboration tools, recovery windows, integrations, and total annual cost.
 SEE: Checklist: Cloud storage management (TechRepublic Premium)
 Best Dropbox alternatives
 Google Drive
 Google Drive is the best overall Dropbox alternative for most users because it combines free cloud storage, real-time collaboration, and tight integration with Google’s productivity tools. Anyone with a Google account can use Drive to store, share, and collaborate on files through Google Docs, Sheets, Slides, Gmail, and Google Workspace.
 For most accounts, the free plan includes 15GB of storage shared across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos. That is far more generous than Dropbox’s free 2GB limit, though users with large photo libraries, email archives, or shared files may still need to upgrade to a paid Google One or Google Workspace plan.
 Google Drive is strongest for collaboration , but it is not the best choice for privacy-focused users. If zero-knowledge encryption or encrypted vault storage is your top priority, Sync, Mega, or NordLocker may be a better fit.
 Key features of Google Drive
 15GB of free storage across Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos.
 Real-time collaboration in Docs, Sheets, and Slides.
 Tight integration with Gmail, Calendar, Meet, and Google Workspace.
 Easy file sharing with permissions and link controls.
 Desktop and mobile apps for cross-device access.
 Visit Google Drive 
 Sync
 Sync is the best Dropbox alternative for privacy-focused teams because it emphasizes secure file storage, encrypted sharing, and stronger privacy controls. This makes it a good fit for businesses and individuals who want to collaborate without giving the provider broad access to stored files.
 Its zero-knowledge encryption is the biggest differentiator. Unlike mainstream storage tools built primarily around productivity ecosystems, Sync is designed for users who want secure file sharing, version history, rollback, and team collaboration with stronger privacy protections.
 Overall, Sync is not as deeply integrated with Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 as Google Drive or OneDrive, but it is a better fit for users who prioritize security over ecosystem convenience.
 Key features of Sync
 Zero-knowledge encryption.
 Secure file sharing and access controls.
 Version history and rollback.
 Team folders and collaboration tools.
 Desktop, web, and mobile access.
 Visit Sync 
 Mega
 Mega is the best Dropbox alternative for free storage allowance. Its free plan offers up to 20 GB of storage, which is more than Dropbox, Google Drive, OneDrive, and many other mainstream cloud storage providers , making it a strong choice for users who need more room without paying right away.
 Mega also stands out for privacy. It offers end-to-end encryption and strong security features, which make it more appealing to users who are uncomfortable storing sensitive files in standard productivity-suite storage tools.
 The trade-off is that Mega may not feel as polished for business collaboration as Google Drive, OneDrive, or Box. It works best for users who want generous free storage, privacy, and flexible syncing rather than built-in productivity apps.
 Key features of Mega
 Generous free storage allowance.
 End-to-end encryption.
 Desktop and mobile apps.
 Flexible syncing options.
 Secure file sharing.
 Visit Mega 
 Microsoft OneDrive
 Microsoft OneDrive is the best Dropbox alternative for Microsoft 365 users . It integrates directly with Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Windows, making it one of the easiest Dropbox replacements for businesses already working in Microsoft’s ecosystem.
 The free version includes 5GB of storage, which is more than Dropbox but less than Google Drive, Mega, pCloud, IDrive, and Icedrive. The real value comes from Microsoft 365 plans, which include OneDrive storage alongside the Microsoft productivity apps many businesses already use.
 However, OneDrive is not the strongest option for zero-knowledge encryption. But it is one of the most practical choices for Windows users and Microsoft-heavy teams who want cloud storage integrated into daily work.
 Key features of Microsoft OneDrive
 5GB of free storage.
 Built into Windows and Microsoft 365.
 Real-time collaboration in Word, Excel, and PowerPoint.
 File sharing, version history, and recovery tools.
 OneDrive Personal Vault for added file protection.
 Visit Microsoft OneDrive 
 pCloud
 pCloud is the best Dropbox alternative for lifetime storage plans. Unlike most cloud storage services that rely only on monthly or annual subscriptions, pCloud offers lifetime plans that can make long-term storage more cost-effective for some users.
 The free plan can offer 10GB of storage, but it requires a series of steps to access it, which can be a hindrance for new users. However, paid plans are available for users who need more space. pCloud also supports file sharing , versioning, media playback, and cross-platform access, making it a strong choice for users with large personal archives, media libraries, or long-term storage needs.
 Privacy-focused users should note that pCloud’s strongest encryption features may require an additional paid option. Still, its lifetime pricing and strong syncing tools make it one of the clearest alternatives to Dropbox for long-term value.
 Key features of pCloud
 10GB of free storage.
 Annual and lifetime storage plans.
 File sharing with link controls.
 File versioning and recovery.
 Built-in media playback and cross-platform apps.
 Visit pCloud 
 IDrive
 IDrive is the best Dropbox alternative for cloud backup. While Dropbox is primarily built for syncing and sharing, IDrive is better suited for users who want to back up computers, phones, servers, and external drives to the cloud.
 To support this, IDrive includes a 10GB free plan and offers strong value for users who need large backup capacity and data storage . It also supports file versioning, recovery, and multi-device backup, making it useful for individuals and businesses that prioritize data protection over document collaboration.
 Still, IDrive is not the best fit if your main priority is real-time co-editing or team document workflows. But if your goal is to protect files across multiple devices, it is one of the strongest Dropbox alternatives.
 Key features of IDrive
 10GB of free storage.
 Cloud backup for multiple devices.
 File versioning and recovery.
 Automatic backup and sync options.
 Support for Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, and Android.
 Visit IDrive 
 Icedrive
 Icedrive is the best Dropbox alternative for users who want a clean interface and virtual drive experience. Its web and app interfaces are easy to navigate, and its Windows virtual drive feature lets users access cloud files in a way that feels closer to using local storage.
 The free plan includes 10GB of storage, which is more generous than Dropbox’s free tier. Paid plans add more storage and encryption features, making Icedrive a good option for users who want simple storage with a modern interface.
 However, Icedrive can be less compelling for teams that need deep collaboration features . Instead, I recommend it for individuals or small teams that prioritize clean design, file previews, fast access, and straightforward cloud storage.
 Key features of Icedrive
 10GB of free storage.
 Clean web and app interface.
 Windows virtual drive functionality.
 File previews for common formats.
 Encryption options on paid plans.
 Visit Icedrive 
 Box
 Box is the best Dropbox alternative for businesses and enterprises. It offers business-focused file sharing, content management, admin controls, security features, workflow tools, and integrations with major productivity platforms.
 Box’s free plan includes 10GB of storage, but the platform is clearly designed for teams and organizations rather than casual individual users. Its business plans are more expensive than some consumer-focused storage services, but they include controls that companies often need, such as permissions, compliance features, workflow automation, and app integrations.
 The biggest reason I recommend Box over Dropbox is enterprise readiness . It is a strong fit for businesses that need file storage, collaboration, governance, and integrations in a secure content management platform.
 Key features of Box
 10GB free individual plan.
 Business file sharing and content management.
 Admin controls and enterprise security features.
 Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 integrations.
 Workflow automation and app integrations.
 Visit Box 
 NordLocker
 NordLocker is the best Dropbox alternative for encrypted file storage. Built by the company behind NordVPN, it focuses on privacy, secure vaults, and encrypted syncing rather than broad productivity-suite collaboration.
 At the same time, NordLocker’s free plan is smaller than many competitors’, but its privacy-first approach makes it useful for users who need to store sensitive files securely. Paid plans offer more storage, cross-device syncing, and access to encrypted file vaults.
 With that said, NordLocker is not the best choice for team document editing or business collaboration. It is strongest for individuals and small teams who want a simple way to encrypt files before syncing them to the cloud.
 Key features of NordLocker
 Encryption-first cloud storage.
 Secure file vaults.
 Automatic cross-platform syncing.
 Zero-knowledge architecture.
 Strong fit for sensitive personal or business files.

 Methodology: How I evaluated Dropbox alternatives
 To evaluate the best Dropbox alternatives, I focused on cloud storage services that can replace or improve on Dropbox’s core functions: file storage, syncing, sharing, collaboration, backup, cross-device access, and security. I prioritized tools that are practical for individuals, freelancers, small teams, and businesses rather than basic storage apps with limited real-world use.
 I also considered why someone might leave Dropbox in 2026. Some users need more free storage, while others want better Microsoft or Google integration, stronger encryption, lower long-term costs, lifetime storage plans, backup features, or enterprise controls. Because these needs vary, I evaluated each provider based on its best-fit use case rather than ranking every tool by storage size alone.
 The main evaluation criteria included:
 Free storage and plan value: I reviewed free storage limits, paid plan pricing, annual discounts, lifetime options, business plans, and whether the provider offers enough value compared with Dropbox.
 File syncing and sharing: I looked at desktop sync, selective sync, folder syncing, link sharing, password-protected links, expiration dates, version history, file requests, and collaboration controls.
 Security and privacy: I considered encryption methods, zero-knowledge or end-to-end encryption options, two-factor authentication, data center policies, compliance features, and privacy-focused design.
 Collaboration tools: I evaluated document editing, team folders, comments, permissions, compatibility with Microsoft Office and Google Workspace, and support for business workflows.
 Platform support: I reviewed availability across Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, web browsers, and desktop sync clients.
 Backup and recovery: I considered automatic backups, file versioning, deleted-file recovery, ransomware protection, and whether the tool works better as backup software or as cloud storage.
 Ease of use: I assessed interface quality, setup experience, file organization, mobile usability, and the ease with which teams or individuals can switch from Dropbox.
 Best-fit use case: I matched each provider to the user or business need it serves best, such as privacy, collaboration, backup, enterprise storage, or low-cost long-term storage.
 I gave more weight to services that provide a clear reason to choose them over Dropbox. For example, Google Drive and OneDrive are strongest for productivity-suite users; Sync and NordLocker are stronger for privacy; pCloud stands out for lifetime storage; IDrive is better for backup; and Box is better for enterprise file management.
 Frequently asked questions (FAQs)
 What is the best free Dropbox alternative?
 Mega offers one of the most generous free storage plans, while Google Drive is the best free Dropbox alternative for collaboration. Google Drive gives users 15GB of free storage across Google Drive, Gmail, and Google Photos, while Mega provides more free storage for users who prioritize capacity and privacy.
 Is Dropbox still worth using?
 Dropbox is still worth using if you value its simple syncing, file sharing, collaboration features, and broad app support. However, users may prefer an alternative if they need more free storage, stronger privacy, lower long-term pricing, deeper Microsoft or Google integration, enterprise controls, or backup-focused features.
 What should I look for in a Dropbox alternative?
 Look for storage limits, pricing, file syncing, sharing controls, version history, deleted file recovery, encryption, platform support, collaboration tools, mobile apps, and integrations with the software you already use. Businesses should also compare admin controls, compliance features, team permissions, and support options.
